punchline: A Vermont janitor out-earned a Wall Street executive over a lifetime, because with money, steady habits count for more than credentials.
thirty_sec: Ronald Read fixed cars for about 25 years and cleaned floors at J.C. Penney for 17 more. He lived so modestly nobody guessed he was rich. When he died in 2014 at 92, he left over $8 million, most of it to his library and hospital. He just saved and held blue-chip stocks for decades. Richard Fuscone, a Harvard-educated Merrill Lynch executive, borrowed heavily for a Greenwich mansion. After 2008 he went bankrupt and lost the house.
question: Why can an amateur so often beat a professional at personal finance, when that almost never happens in other fields?
